title: Circular dependency involving ReprEnum not handled correctly
body_truncated:
A recent PR in typeshed has exposed a bug in pyright's handling of circular dependencies between classes. See [this thread](https://github.com/python/typeshed/pull/10216) for details.

The `ReprEnum` class derives from `Enum` which uses the metaclass `EnumMeta`. The `EnumMeta` has a `__new__` method that describes a keyword parameter `boundary` of type `FlagBoundary`. This type derives from `StrEnum` which derives from `ReprEnum`, and we're back to the start.

title: Pyright doesn't detect coroutine awaits properly.
body_truncated:
I've run across a rather odd behavior in pyright's `async/await` detection.

Here's a test case
```
class TestCase:
    async def test_fn(self, r):
        return {}

    async def case1(self):
        b = []
        m = await self.test_fn(b)
        m["test"]

    async def case2(self):
        m = await self.test_fn([])
        m["test"]

    async def case3(self):
        m = await self.test_fn(None)
        m["test"]
```

title: Pyright fails to report unnecessary `# type: ignore` comments for previously-cached files after clearing type cache
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
We are currently running Pyright on a medium-sized codebase of ~5,000 files. We have a large number of `# type: ignore` comments after running a codemod to integrate Pyright's strict ruleset with line-level ignores. When we run Pyright, the heap is predictably cleared at 90% usage; however, this also clears all of the parsed results required to validate unnecessary `# type: ignore` comments.

In short:

```
NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=8192" pyright .

1389 errors, 1 warning, 0 informations # 1378 'Unnecessary "# pyright: ignore" comment' errors

pyright .

Emptying type cache to avoid heap overflow. Used 3731MB out of 4144MB.
12 errors, 1 warning, 0 informations # 1 'Unnecessary "# pyright: ignore" comment' error
```

I think it's possible that the diagnostics return early based on https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/719ddea20a1ed545f4a29119d66a08b5999469b8/packages/pyright-internal/src/analyzer/sourceFile.ts#L436, which has already been cleared by https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/719ddea20a1ed545f4a29119d66a08b5999469b8/packages/pyright-internal/src/analyzer/program.ts#L1015. If that is the case, then maybe Pyright needs to collect diagnostics after analyzing each file rather than in a second step after all analysis has concluded?

We've fixed the issue by bumping V8's egregiously tiny heap size (which I understand is necessary for pointer compression, but still). We're also planning on whittling down the `# type: ignore` comments. I'd love to get your perspective on the issue, though, because this seems like something that requires some restructuring of the analysis phase based on my layman's knowledge.

We love your type checker, btw! Such a great tool.

**To Reproduce**
Set up a large repository with a significant amount of `# type: ignore` comments, throttle the V8 heap size, enable `reportUnnecessaryTypeIgnoreComment`, run `pyright .`, note that unnecessary comments are flagged when analyzing in

body_truncated:
With code like this:

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Generic, TypeVar

A = TypeVar("A")
@dataclass()
class DcWrapper(Generic[A]):
    value: A

test1: DcWrapper[int] | DcWrapper[str] = DcWrapper(1) # Errors, unexpectedly
test2: DcWrapper[int] | DcWrapper[str] = DcWrapper("ab")
test3: DcWrapper[int] | DcWrapper[str] = DcWrapper(None) # Errors, as expected

class Wrapper(Generic[A]):
    def __init__(self, value: A) -> None:
        self.value = value

test4: Wrapper[int] | Wrapper[str] = Wrapper(1)
test5: Wrapper[int] | Wrapper[str] = Wrapper("ab")
test6: Wrapper[int] | Wrapper[str] = Wrapper(None) # Errors, as expected

pyright 1.1.310 reports:

title: "reportImplicitOverride" gets confused by wrapper function with inferred return type
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
If result type of a wrapper function is omitted (so that a function can be returned instead of a callable), and an overriding method is annotated by it, the returned function inside the wrapper function is incorrectly required to be annotated with `@override`.

**To Reproduce**
See sample code below.

As a non-overriding method and an overriding method get annotated with a same function, adding a `@override` or not will both get an error.

**Expected behavior**
`__eq__` needs `@override`. `wrapped` inside `wrap` doesn't need `@override`.

**Screenshots or Code**
```python
# pyright: strict
# pyright: reportImplicitOverride=true

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Callable, TypeVar
from typing_extensions import override

T = TypeVar("T")

def wrap(func: Callable[..., Any], /):
    def wrapped(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        raise NotImplementedError
    
    return wrapped

class C:
    @wrap
    def f(self, /) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError
    
    @override
    @wrap
    def __eq__(self, other: object, /) -> bool:
        raise NotImplementedError
```

title: Wrong django's TextChoices.value after 1.1.307
body_truncated:
First of all, the expansion of `Enum.value` to its literal options is really nice!

But I just faced an issue with a django's TextChoices: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/ref/models/fields/#enumeration-types

Those are implemented as a subclass of enum, but supports receiving the value as a tuple of `(value, label)`.

With 1.1.307 this code produces the following:

```python
from django.db import models


class MyEnum(models.TextChoices):
    FOO = "foo", "Foo option"
    BAR = "bar", "bar option"

# obs. the correct type for this would be Literal['foo'] (or at least a generic str)
reveal_type(MyEnum.FOO.value)  # Type of "MyEnum.FOO.value" is "tuple[Literal['foo'], Literal['Foo option']]"
# this is still works fine
reveal_type(MyEnum.FOO.label)  # Type of "MyEnum.FOO.label" is "str"

def foo(x: MyEnum):
    # obs. the correct type for this would be Literal['foo'] | Literal['bar'] (or at least a generic str)
    reveal_type(x.value)  # Type of "x.value" is "tuple[Literal['foo'], Literal['Foo option']] | tuple[Literal['bar'], Literal['bar option']]"
    # this is still works fine
    reveal_type(x.label)  # Type of "x.label" is "str"
```

Those seems to be even overriding the typing defined in the stubs that I'm using in here: https://github.com/sbdchd/django-types/blob/main/django-stubs/db/models/enums.pyi#L36

Don't know if this is something that pyright can workaround, but if it is not, how can the stub typing be fixed in order to support this?

title: Deprecated decorator false positive
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
PEP 702 proposes an introduction of a new `@deprecated` decorator, which pyright already seems to be recognizing. This is fine when it's imported from `typing_extensions`, however pyright also treats custom functions named "`deprecated`" in the same way.

**To Reproduce**
1. Create a custom function named `deprecated`
2. Use this function as to decorate another function
3. Notice the decorated function was marked deprecated

**Expected behavior**
I'm not sure this is actually a bug, or if it was introduced as a feature to support other implementations of deprecated. However I'm assuming it's a bug, and if so, only the deprecated decorator actually imported from `typing_extensions` (or later `typing`) should be marking a function as deprecated, custom implementations might not act the same way, in fact they might not even be decorators.

That said, it would probably be pretty weird for someone to implement a function called `deprecated` that's not a decorator, and this could actually be useful for custom implementations, so perhaps it's worth keeping around as a feature, I'm only reporting this since I haven't seen any mention of this being a feature, so in case this isn't supposed to happen, it might be worth addressing.

title: Regression with Overloads and lambda
Calling `list()` on `urllib.parse.urlparse()` produces a generic type
body_truncated:
### Discussed in https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/discussions/5035
Originally posted by **Pyprohly** April 29, 2023 Before Pyright version 1.1.295, the following code was legal: ```python import urllib.parse url = "https://www.google.com?a=1&b=2" urlparts = list(urllib.parse.urlparse(url)) urlparts[4] = "a=1&b=2&c=3" url = urllib.parse.urlunparse(urlparts) ``` Pyright (1.1.305) now reports the type of `urlparts` as `list[AnyStr@_ParseResultBase]` instead of `list[str]` as it used to be, making the above code illegal. On the other hand, Mypy (1.2.0) still reports the type as `list[str]`. I understand that this was caused by [a change in typeshed][1], but the code I’ve written above seems reasonable enough, and it’s not obvious to me what the type of doing `list()` on a generic `NamedTuple` should be. [1]: https://github.com/python/typeshed/commit/bc847a9b07948a20fcd06ad6c19f2e73437e957e Is the error reporting for the above code correct? How do I fix the code? title: pyright 1.1.302 unable to solve TypeVar in some situations
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
In a library I am developing I'm using a (somewhat complex) set of generic container-like classes and functions that operate on them. I noticed when writing test cases using `assert_type` that pyright 1.1.302 can fail to solve TypeVars depending on whether one uses intermediate variables or not in calls. This is a regression from pyright 1.1.301 that worked independent of how the code is structured.

**To Reproduce**
Some container-like types that use generics and overloads
```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar, assert_type, Type, overload

T = TypeVar("T")
T1 = TypeVar("T1")
T2 = TypeVar("T2")

class Box(Generic[T]):
    def wrap(self, type: Type[T1]) -> "Box[T1]": ...

class Crate(Generic[T]):
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, box1: Box[T1]) -> "Crate[tuple[T1]]": ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, box1: Box[T1], box2: Box[T2]) -> "Crate[tuple[T1, T2]]": ...

Container = Box[T] | Crate[T]

def unpack(x: Container[T]) -> T: ...
```

test cases where I noticed the issue

```python
# works as expected
def example1() -> None:
    item = Crate(Box().wrap(int))  # revealed_type is Crate[tuple[int]]
    assert_type(unpack(item), tuple[int])

# same example but without intermediate variable assignments; fails using pyright 1.1.302 
def example2() -> None:
    # "assert_type" mismatch: expected "tuple[int]" but received "T@unpack" (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
    assert_type(unpack(Crate(Box().wrap(int))), tuple[int])

```

**VS Code extension or command-line**
I am running pyright (both 1.1.301 and 1.1.302) using https://pypi.org/project/pyright/ and pyright 1.1.301 in VS Code using the pylance extension.

title: non-literal floats capture all in match statements
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

I am not completely sure this is a bug but it seems like one to me. If a float is not typed as a `Literal`, then it captures all the floats in a `match` statement. See the example below. My guess is this was done so `float()` catches all the floats? But that seems like a special case that should be handled instead of assuming everything that has the type `float` will catch all the cases.

**To Reproduce**

I am on the pyright version 1.1.301.

```python
from typing_extensions import reveal_type


class SpecialNumbers:
    SUPRISE_NUMBER = 123
    INFINITY = float("inf")  # I cannot find a way to represent an infinity with Literal...
    ZERO = float()  # This type could be infered as `Literal[0.0]`. But it's `float` instead.


def parse_float(s: str):
    match float(s):
        case SpecialNumbers.SUPRISE_NUMBER:
            return "Hahaha"
        case SpecialNumbers.INFINITY:  # If you comment this case out you'll see the "Never" become "float" below.
            raise NotImplementedError()
        # case SpecialNumbers.ZERO:  # This is another case that behaves like the INFINITY above.
        #     return "zero"
        case f:
            reveal_type(f)  # Type of "f" is "Never"
            return f

# Some useful checks for verify understanding of the actual behavior...
print(parse_float("100"))
print(parse_float("0"))
print(parse_float("123"))
```

**Expected behavior**

I expect the only cases that match all floats to be `float()` or a new variable declared in the match case (`case my_new_float:`). Everything else such as `math.inf` should pass the rest of the floats on to the next case.

Thanks for much for working in Pyright! It's awesome.

title: Unexpected Generic[] behavior with LiteralString-bounded TypeVar
body_truncated:
Hi!

I'm seeing some interesting behavior on pyright `1.1.300` when bounding a `TypeVar` with `LiteralString`. Here's a quick example that type checks without errors:
```python
import dataclasses
from typing import Generic, LiteralString, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


@dataclasses.dataclass
class Container(Generic[T]):
    """Dummy generic class."""
    inner: T


TLiteralString = TypeVar("TLiteralString", bound=LiteralString)


def wrap_with_default(
    x: TLiteralString | None,
    default: TLiteralString,
) -> Container[TLiteralString]:
    """Wrap an input with a dummy container object."""
    if x is None:
        x = default  # `x` should now be narrowed to TLiteralString.
    return Container(x)
```

Unexpectedly, this breaks when I simply swap the final return statement for an assignment followed by a return:

```python
import dataclasses
from typing import Generic, LiteralString, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


@dataclasses.dataclass
class Container(Generic[T]):
    """Dummy generic class."""
    inner: T


TLiteralString = TypeVar("TLiteralString", bound=LiteralString)


def wrap_with_default(
    x: TLiteralString | None,
    default: TLiteralString,
) -> Container[TLiteralString]:
    """Wrap an input with a dummy container object."""
    if x is None:
        x = default
    out = Container(x)  # New
    return out  # New
```

Where the final line now gives me the error: `Expression of type "Container[TLiteralString@wrap_with_default | str]" cannot be assigned to return type "Container[TLiteralString@wrap_with_default]"`. In contrast, mypy runs without errors for both examples.

As additional notes, this issue disappears when I:
- Remove the `LiteralString` bound.
- Use `Tuple[TLiteralString]` instead of my custom `Container[TLiteralString]`.

title: ParamSpec-based signature change works with functions but not classes
body_truncated:
Hi!

I'm running into an issue where a `ParamSpec`-based signature works for function inputs, but breaks for a class that has the exact same signature.

**Background**

I have an application with a method `f()` that has an extremely vague signature:
```python
class Class:
    def f(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
        print(args, kwargs)
```


And I want to write a decorator that populates the signature of `f` by borrowing from another function (evokes functools.wraps):

```python
def dummy_f(a: str, b: float) -> None:
    ...

class Class:
    @replace_signature_with(func_with_desired_signature)
    def f(self, *args, **kwargs) -> None:
        print(args, kwargs)
```

Since `f()` is a method, I wrote a decorator that concatenates `Class` as the first argument to a ParamSpec. So `dummy_f`'s signature `(a: str, b: float)` gets transformed into `(self: Class, a: str, b: float)`:

```python
def replace_signature_with(
    func_with_desired_signature: Callable[P, Any]
) -> Callable[[Callable], Callable[Concatenate[Class, P], None]]:
    """Decorator for replacing the signature of a function with that of some other function."""
    return lambda f: f  # type: ignore
```

Putting everything together, this works great!

```python

import dataclasses
from typing import Any, Callable, Concatenate, ParamSpec, cast

P = ParamSpec("P")


def replace_signature_with(
    func_with_desired_signature: Callable[P, Any]
) -> Callable[[Callable], Callable[Concatenate[Class, P], None]]:

title: Auto-variance calculation doesn't take into account manually-specified variance of base class type parameters
body_truncated:
The auto-variance calculation implemented for PEP 695 does not currently take into account the case where a new-style generic class derives from an old-style generic class where the variance of a type parameter is manually specified.

In the example below, `T1@A` is invariant, so `T@B` should be inferred to be invariant as well, but currently it is inferred as covariant.

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar

T1 = TypeVar("T1")
T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)

class A(Generic[T1]):
    pass

class B[T](A[T]):
    ...

def func(a: B[int], b: B[float]):
    # The type parameter for B should be invariant,
    # so both of these assignments should generate
    # an error. Currently, only one of them does.
    if 1 < 2:
        a = b
    else:
        b = a
```

title: Invalid return type inference in function with multiple return points
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Invalid type inference for function return types if multiple type of dictionaries are returned and one of them is initiated with an empty `dict`. Pyright only considers one of the return points for inferring the return type, ignoring the empty dictionary type which is `dict[Unknown, Unknown]`.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior: open code in vscode with pyright extension 
```python
def foo(error: bool): # inferred type: (function) def foo(error: bool) -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]
    result = {}
    if error:
        return {"error": {"message": "some message"}}
    result["list"] = []
    return result

def bar(error: bool): # inferred type: (function) def foo(error: bool) -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]
    result = {}
    if not error:
        result["list"] = []
        return result
    return {"error": {"message": "some message"}}

result = foo(False) # same for bar(...)
result["list"].append("something") # error: Cannot access member "append" for type "dict[str, str]"
```

**Expected behavior**
Instead of `dict[str, dict[str, str]]` should infer `dict[str, dict[str, str]]|dict[Unknown, Unknown]` to avoid misleading error messages at the calling point of the function.

title: pyright complains overload will never be used because parameters overlap
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

I'm trying to express two possible scenarios that my function could take as one of the parameters:

1. A type with implements `__radd__` and returns it's own type
2. A type with implements `__radd__` and does not returns it's own type


**To Reproduce**

1. Write a Python file like this:

```python
from typing import Protocol, Any, TypeVar, overload

class RAddable(Protocol):
    def __radd__(self: "RAddable", other: Any, /) -> Any:
        ...

T = TypeVar("T")
class SameRAddable(Protocol):
    def __radd__(self: T, other: Any, /) -> T:
        ...

RA = TypeVar("RA", bound=SameRAddable)

@overload
def add(a: Any, b: RA) -> RA:
    ...

@overload
def add(a: Any, b: RAddable) -> Any:
    ...

def add(a: Any, b: Any) -> Any:
    return a + b
```

2. Run pyright on this file

3. Get the following error on the second overload:

```
Overload 2 for "add" will never be used because its parameters overlap overload 1Pylance[reportOverlappingOverload](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/configuration.md#reportOverlappingOverload)
```


**Expected behavior**

While the second overload does overlap with the first overload, it isn't completely overlapped. In particular if `__radd__` explictly returns a different type, e.g.:

```python
class Foo:
    pass

class Bar:
    def __radd__(self: Self, other: Any) -> str:
        return "Hello World"

print(add(Foo(), Bar()))
```

Bar here clearly does not match overload 1, but does match overload 2.


**Additional context**

It doesn't seem to be possible in current Python type hinting to express the return type of overload 2 as "Not RA", but I do appreciate this might be a design choice and not a bug in pyright.

title: Intransitivity in TypeAlias handling with `cast`
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

The new handling of `TypeAlias` requirements introduces an intransitivity when working with `cast`-ed types.

**To Reproduce**

Consider the two following snippets of code.

```py
from typing import cast, TypeAlias

Obj: TypeAlias = cast(type[object], object)
x: Obj
```

and 

```py
from typing import cast, TypeAlias

_Obj = cast(type[object], object)
Obj: TypeAlias = _Obj
x: Obj
```

One would presume that both of these are equivalent (modulo beta-reduction I guess?) and that pyright would report the same set of errors on both. 

However, the former produces an error (`error: Invalid expression form for type alias definition`), whereas the latter does not. 

**Expected behavior**

I'm not totally sure what the respective PEPs say, but my desire would be for bot of these to be legal. While I recognize that expressions are not normally permitted for type aliases, in the case of a cast I would expect it to work (for context, we use this to retype SQLAlchemy tables' instances).

Regardless of whether that would be permitted, I would expect the two variants to have the same output.

**VS Code extension or command-line**

pyright (yarn, `1.1.293`)

```python

from typing import TypeVar

X = TypeVar("X")

    to_add = [value, str(value)]
    return to_add


def add_to_list_silent(value: X) -> list[X]:
    """Inline return: does pass type-check :("""

title: Pyright does not correctly parse toml `[[listsOfDictionaries]]`
body_truncated:
The following TOML snippets map to identical JSON (can confirm [here](https://pseitz.github.io/toml-to-json-online-converter/)). See also the [TOML spec](https://toml.io/en/v1.0.0#array-of-tables).

```
[[executionEnvironments]]
root = "src/sub"
```

```
executionEnvironments = [
  { root = "src/sub" },
]
```

However, pyright does not interpret them identically. Below is a repro zsh script that works on macOS:

```
#!/usr/bin/env zsh

local projroot=$(mktemp -d /tmp/temp.XXXX)
pushd $projroot >/dev/null

cat > pyproject.toml <<EOF
[tool.pyright]

include = [
  "src"
]

# (syntax 1)
executionEnvironments = [
  { root = "src/sub" },
]
EOF

# sub this in (syntax 2) for (syntax 1) above

# (syntax 2)
# [[executionEnvironments]]
# root = "src/sub"

mkdir src
mkdir src/sub
mkdir src/sub/foo

cat > src/sub/foo/__init__.py <<EOF
import fake
EOF

pyright --verbose src

popd >/dev/null
rm -rf $projroot
```

Run this once and you should approximately this in the output:

```
Found 1 source file
Could not import 'fake' in file '/private/tmp/temp.fDZA/src/sub/foo/__init__.py'
  ...
  Looking in root directory of execution environment '/private/tmp/temp.xzO8/src/sub'
```

Now sub in syntax (2) for syntax (1) and run again, you should see:

```
Found 1 source file
Could not import 'fake' in file '/private/tmp/temp.fDZA/src/sub/foo/__init__.py'
  ...
  Looking in root directory of execution environment '/private/tmp/temp.xzO8'
```

The execution environment root directory is not as-specified-- I think the specified `[[executionEnvironments]]` is being ignored completely.

Looks like the TOML parser used by pyright is old and unmaintained: https://github.com/iarna/iarna-toml. Pyright should switch to a [1.0-compliant parser](https://github.com/toml-lang/toml/wiki#v100-compliant).

**Describe the bug**

from typing import Hashable, TypeVar, Sequence

HashableT = TypeVar("HashableT", bound=Hashable)

class Foo:

    @property

        return self._something

    @something.setter
    def something(self, newthing: list[HashableT]):
        self._something = newthing

    def set_something(self, newthing: list[HashableT]):
        self._something = newthing


f = Foo()
f.something = ["a", "b", "c"]
f.set_something(["a", "b", "c"])
```

title: `reportPrivateImportUsage` error from exported import of an imported name
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

Hi! I'm coming from https://github.com/google/jaxtyping/pull/49, where we're running into some unexpected behavior with importing names that seem properly exported in an `__init__.py`.

It's probably best explained with an example --

When try to import certain names from our package, in this case `exporttest`, we're running into a reportPrivateImportUsage error:
```python
# try_import.py
from exporttest import _Assigned  # OK
from exporttest import Imported   # reportPrivateImportUsage error!
```

However, in `exporttest/__init__.py`, both names are actually exported using the `import X as X` convention!
```python
# exporttest/__init__.py
from .src import _Assigned as _Assigned
from .src import Imported as Imported
```

The difference ends up being how `Imported` and `_Assigned` are initially defined:
```python
# exporttest/src.py
from typing import List
from typing import List as Imported

_Assigned = List
```

**To Reproduce**
I've put a minimum example for reproducing this error in this repo: https://github.com/brentyi/jaxtyping-export-repro

**Expected behavior**
To be honest, I'm not entirely sure that this is a bug, but it's weird that the internal `exporttest <=> exporttest.src` interface is impacting the `exporttest <=> try_import.py` interface.

The short-term solution is to stick with the `_Assigned = List` pattern for making aliases, but this breaks for special types like `Annotated`. Adding an `__all__ = ["Imported", "_Assigned"]` to `src.py` also works (this is how https://github.com/google/jaxtyping/pull/49 currently suppresses the error), but feels cumbersome.

Is this considered a bug? Any suggestions for working around it?

**VS Code extension or command-line**
I'm running `pyright try_import.py` with `pyright 1.1.282`.


---

cc @patrick-kidger

title: Incorrect checking of generic local functions
body_truncated:
In this example:

```python
from typing import Callable, Optional, TypeVar

T = TypeVar('T')

def make_id() -> Callable[[T], T]:
    x: Optional[T] = None
    def not_id(y: T) -> T:
        nonlocal x
        if x is None:
            x = y
        return x
    return not_id

id = make_id()

reveal_type(id('hest'))
reveal_type(id(3.14159))
```
It will reveal `str`, `float` but the code will actually return `str` both times.  It looks like the return type annotation is causing `T` to appear bound in the body but that isn't right.  It should occur free both in `x: Optional[T]` and the signature `(y: T) -> T`.

The expected behavior is similar to the corresponding example with the initialization of `x` lifted out and `nonlocal` changed to `global`, which does report `error: Type variable "T" has no meaning in this context (reportGeneralTypeIssues)`.

**Describe the bug**
An empty set or list inside a tuple used as a function parameter typed as `Iterable[_T]` (where `_T` is a `TypeVar`) will result in `reportUnknownArgumentType`. This does not happen inside of lists. **To Reproduce**

from typing_extensions import TypeVar

_T = TypeVar("_T")
def foo(_: Iterable[Any]) -> None: ...

foo(["A", "B", ()])
foo(["A", "B", []])
foo(["A", "B", {}])
foo(("A", "B", ()))
foo(("A", "B", []))
foo(("A", "B", {}))

bar(["A", "B", ()])
bar(["A", "B", []])
bar(["A", "B", {}])
bar(("A", "B", ()))
bar(("A", "B", []))  # error reportUnknownArgumentType
bar(("A", "B", {}))  # error reportUnknownArgumentType

No error (empty set infered as `dict[Any, Any]` and empty list as `list[Any]`), like all the other calls

title: Pyright does not resolve some imports that python resolves
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Pyright does not resolve some imports that python resolves.

**To Reproduce**
* Set up the initial state via the following shell script (run in a new directory):
```sh
# Create a fake repository
mkdir repo
echo "from foo.bar import Bar" > repo/bug.py
cat > repo/pyrightconfig.json << EOF
{
    "executionEnvironments": [
        {
            "root": "."
        }
    ],
    "venv": "venv",
    "venvPath": ".."
}
EOF
 
# Create a venv
python -m venv venv
 
# Go to the site-packages directory
cd venv/lib/python*/site-packages
 
# Create fake "foo.bar" packages (via .pth files)
mkdir -p Bar2/foo/bar
echo "Bar2" > Bar2.pth
mkdir -p Bar3/foo/bar
cat > Bar3/foo/bar/__init__.py << EOF
class Bar:
    pass
EOF
echo "Bar3" > Bar3.pth
```
* Notice that Pyright does not resolve `Bar` in `repo/bug.py`.
* Run `./venv/bin/python` and notice that `from foo.bar import Bar` works there.

**Expected behavior**
Pyright should resolve `foo.bar.Bar`, like Python does.

**Additional context**
Interestingly, the bug does NOT happen when doing any of the following things on the initial state:
* Delete the empty `Bar2/foo/bar` directory. This suggests that the bug is related to namespace packages.
* Rename `Bar3.pth` as `Bar1.pth`. This suggests that the order of discovery matters.
* Reduce the package "depth" (i.e. use `bar` everywhere instead of `foo.bar`).

title: wrong type inferred for Tuple[T, ...] + Tuple[*Ts]
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

pyright says `Tuple[T, ...] + Tuple[*Ts]` has a type `Tuple[T | *Ts, ...]`, while left-right swapped `Tuple[*Ts] + Tuple[T, ...]` has a type `Tuple[Union[*Ts] | T, ...]`.

iterating over first one, element type is `T | object`. not the expected one `T | Union[*Ts]`.

**To Reproduce**

```python3
from typing import Tuple, TypeVar, Iterable, Union
from typing_extensions import TypeVarTuple, reveal_type, Unpack

T = TypeVar("T")
Ts = TypeVarTuple("Ts")
Us = TypeVarTuple("Us")

def f(x: "Tuple[T, ...]", y: "Tuple[*Ts]"):
    reveal_type(x + y)
    for e in x + y:
        reveal_type(e)
        yield e

reveal_type(f)

def good(x: "Tuple[T, ...]", y: "Tuple[*Ts]"):
    reveal_type(y + x)
    for e in y + x:
        reveal_type(e)
        yield e

reveal_type(good)
```
```
information: Type of "x + y" is "tuple[T@f | *Ts@f, ...]"
information: Type of "e" is "T@f | object"
warning: TypeVar "T" appears only once in generic function signature (reportInvalidTypeVarUse)
warning: TypeVar "Ts" appears only once in generic function signature (reportInvalidTypeVarUse)
information: Type of "f" is "(x: Tuple[T@f, ...], y: Tuple[*Ts@f]) -> Generator[T@f | object, None, None]"
information: Type of "y + x" is "tuple[Union[*Ts@good] | T@good, ...]"
information: Type of "e" is "Union[*Ts@good] | T@good"
warning: TypeVar "T" appears only once in generic function signature (reportInvalidTypeVarUse)
warning: TypeVar "Ts" appears only once in generic function signature (reportInvalidTypeVarUse)

**Expected behavior**

* `x + y` in `f` shoud have the type `Tuple[T | Union[*Ts], ...]`

title: Returning Covariant class in Generic Protocols gives warning message
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
If we return a class instead of a bounded instance in a Generic Protocol method, we get a warning about the covariant nature of the class. Making the class invariant asses pyright check and fails mypy check.

--

According to PEP-0544, generic protocols can have methods that return an instance of a covariant type:

https://peps.python.org/pep-0544/#generic-protocols

```python
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar
T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)


class Box(Protocol[T_co]):
    def content(self) -> T_co: ):
        ...
```

As far as I could understand from the example below in the PEP, the TypeVar cannot be a covariant if it is assigned to a mutable attribute.

```python
class Proto(Protocol[T]):
    attr: T  # this class is invariant, since it has a mutable attribute
```

If I use `Type[T]` as the return type of a method, Pyright says that it needs to be invariant. 

But if I change my code to `covariant=False`, the warning in pyright is gone but I get this error from Mypy:

```
generic_protocol.py:6: error: Invariant type variable "T" used in protocol where covariant one is expected
 [misc]
    class Box(Protocol[T]):
    ^
```

The PEP also states that:

> To distinguish between protocol class variables and protocol instance variables, the special ClassVar annotation should be used as specified by [PEP 526](https://peps.python.org/pep-0526). By default, protocol variables as defined above are considered readable and writable. To define a read-only protocol variable, one can use an (abstract) property.

And If I try to use `T` as ClassVar, I get the warning
> "ClassVar" type cannot include type variables (Pyright reportGeneralTypeIssues)

If I use the strategy suggested by the pep (below), I get no complaints from pyright, but mypy also gives me:
> error: Invariant type variable "T_co" used in protocol where covariant one is expected
 [misc] 

```python
from abc import abstractmethod
fro

title: Synthesized `__dataclass_fields__` should be a `ClassVar`
body_truncated:
Pyright synthesizes a field called `__dataclass_fields__` for dataclass and dataclass-like (PEP 681) classes.

It currently declares this synthesized field as a normal class-level variable (i.e. a class variable that can be overridden by an instance variable). It should probably be a `ClassVar`. Mypy models it as such.

See mypy issue https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/14029 for more context.

        self.value = None

    def func(self, param: int):

The same behavior can also be reproduced with functions and global variables, and as such is not specific to instance attributes.

**Expected behavior**

title: Weird interaction with `LiteralString` and f-strings

**Describe the bug**
Conditional variable binding interacts unexpectedly with LiteralString f-strings.

**To Reproduce**
See attached code snippet.

**Expected behavior**
I expected f-string interpolation and string concatenation to be treated similarly.

**Screenshots or Code**
If applicable, add screenshots or the text of the code (surrounded by triple back ticks) to help explain your problem.
```python

baz: LiteralString

if 1 == 1:
    foo = "foo"
    baz = f"I am {foo}"  # OK
else:
    foo = "bar"

x: MyList[int] = MyList([1, 2, 3])
append_float(x)
```

The problem here is that `T` is covariant, but it's being used in a base class `list` whose corresponding type parameter is invariant. This means usage of the resulting subclass `MyList` can now violate the variance of its base class.

A type checker should catch this case and report an error.

This was discovered in this [typeshed issue](https://github.com/python/typeshed/pull/8781).

title: Structural pattern matching on polymorphic arguments forgets type variable binding in some cases
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

When using `match` on a polymorphic argument, on `case` branches that are subtypes of that polymorphic type, pyright forgets that the type variable has been bound.

**To Reproduce**

In the example below, all the type assignments are correct except `case B(xs): ....`. When the `if isinstance` block is uncommented, the type assigned to `xs` in the `case` changes unexpectedly (but the assigned type is still incorrect).

```python
from typing import Generic, List, TypeVar

T = TypeVar('T')

class A(Generic[T]):
    __match_args__ = ('xs',)
    xs: List[T]

class B(A[T]):
    pass

def f(a: A[T], a_: A[int], b: B[T]) -> None:
    match b: # no problem, case branches aren't subtypes of b's type
        case B(xs): print(xs) # xs: List[T@f]

    match a_: # no problem, not polymorphic
        case B(xs): print(xs) # xs: List[int]
        case A(xs): print(xs) # xs: List[int]

    # if isinstance(a, B):          # Uncommenting this causes pyright to assign the type
    #     a.xs # a.xs: List[T@f]    # `xs: List[T@f] | List[Unknown]` in the case B(xs)
                                    # branch below

    match a:
        case B(xs): print(xs) # xs: List[Unknown] <-- incorrect
        case A(xs): print(xs) # xs: List[T@f]
```

**Expected behavior**

The assigned type should be `List[T@f]`.

**Screenshots or Code**

See above.

title: `Unpacked` `Any` `tuple` doesn't match against `TypeVarTuple`, contrary to PEP-646
body_truncated:
I believe that `Foo(Unpack[tuple[Any, ...]])` should be an acceptable type for `Foo(Unpack[Xs])` with `TypeVarTuple("Xs")`. Pyright does not accept this kind of code.

PEP-646 has code very similar to:
```py
from typing import Any, Generic, NewType, cast
from typing_extensions import TypeVarTuple, Unpack

Shape = TypeVarTuple("Shape")
Batch = NewType("Batch", int)
Height = NewType("Height", int)
Width = NewType("Width", int)
Channels = NewType("Channels", int)

class Array(Generic[Unpack[Shape]]): ...

y: Array[Unpack[tuple[Any, ...]]] = cast(Array[Unpack[tuple[Any, ...]]], None)

def expect_variadic_array(
    x: Array[Batch, Unpack[Shape]]
) -> None: ...

expect_variadic_array(y)  # Suppose to be okay according to PEP-646 but fails to type check in pyright

def expect_precise_array(
    x: Array[Batch, Height, Width, Channels]
) -> None: ...

expect_precise_array(y)  # OK
```
In the PEP, `expect_variadic_array(y)` is supposed to type check. With the pyright CLI v1.1.269, it raises the following error:
```
error: Argument of type "Array[*tuple[Any, ...]]" cannot be assigned to parameter "x" of type "Array[Batch, *Shape@expect_variadic_array]" in function "expect_variadic_array"
    TypeVar "Shape@Array" is invariant
      TypeVarTuple cannot be bound to a tuple of unknown length (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```

This code also type checks in pyre 0.9.15.

But the presence of a specific error message suggests that pyright has chosen to diverge from the spec? The behavior specified in the PEP seems quite useful for doing incremental upgrades to shaped arrays (e.g. using `NDArray: TypeAlias = ndarray[Unpack[tuple[Any, ...]], DType]`).

title: Different order of items in `Union[Callable[[], T], Callable[[], Awaitable[T]]]` results in different behavior
body_truncated:
This is kind of a tricky issue that showed up with Pyright 1.1.266. I can't say I fully understand it, but I'll illustrate with an example.

I have a function that takes a parameter with type:

```
Union[Callable[[], T], Callable[[], Awaitable[T]]]
```

When the order of the types in the `Union` is reversed, like this:

```
Union[Callable[[], Awaitable[T]], Callable[[], T]])
```

... then Pyright has different behavior with type narrowing. This started happening with 1.1.266.

Here's an example that shows the change in behavior. The function `call2` previously did not result in Pyright errors, but it does now.

```py
# pyright: reportUnusedExpression=false

from typing import Callable, Union, Awaitable, TypeVar, cast
from typing_extensions import TypeGuard
import inspect

T = TypeVar("T")


def is_async_callable(
    obj: Union[Callable[..., T], Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]]
) -> TypeGuard[Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]]:
    """
    Returns True if `obj` is an `async def` function, or if it's an object with a
    `__call__` method which is an `async def` function.
    """
    if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(obj):
        return True
    if hasattr(obj, "__call__"):  # noqa: B004
        if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(obj.__call__):  # type: ignore
            return True

    return False


async def call(fn: Union[Callable[[], T], Callable[[], Awaitable[T]]]) -> T:
    if is_async_callable(fn):
        fn
        # Inferred type with 1.1.265: (parameter) fn: (...) -> Awaitable[T@call]
        # Inferred type with 1.1.266: (parameter) fn: (...) -> Awaitable[T@call]

        return await fn()  # OK
    else:
        # cast() is needed because TypeGuard doesn't support negative type narrowing.
        # (This is expected behavior)
        fn = cast(Callable[[], T], fn)
        return fn()


async def call2(fn: Union[Callable[[], Awaitable[T]], Callable[[], T]]) -> T:
    if is_async_callable(fn):

title: Using assert_type on type parameter of a generic: Unknown vs. Any
body_truncated:
We're trying something with generics in pandas-stubs, and have noticed a difference in behavior with `pyright` and `mypy` that we'd like to reconcile.

Consider this type stub, called `genericret.pyi`:
```python
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Generic, TypeVar, overload

S1 = TypeVar("S1", int, str)

class Foo(Generic[S1]):
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, dtype: type[S1]) -> Foo[S1]: ...
    @overload
    def __new__(cls, dtype=...) -> Foo: ...
    def func(self) -> S1: ...
```
And this test python code `genrectst.py`:
```python
from typing_extensions import assert_type, reveal_type

from genericret import Foo
from typing import Any

f = Foo(int)
reveal_type(f)
reveal_type(f.func())

g = Foo()
reveal_type(g)
reveal_type(g.func())

assert_type(g.func(), Any)
```

In this case, if a `dtype` is specified, we can say that we know the specific type of `Foo`.  But if `dtype` is not specified, then it is unknown.  But that's OK - except we want the function `func()` to then return `Any` as a type, which is what `mypy` does. 

`mypy` output:
```text
genrectst.py:7: note: Revealed type is "genericret.Foo[builtins.int]"
genrectst.py:8: note: Revealed type is "builtins.int"
genrectst.py:11: note: Revealed type is "genericret.Foo[Any]"
genrectst.py:12: note: Revealed type is "Any"
Success: no issues found in 1 source file
```

`pyright` output:
```text
  genrectst.py:7:13 - information: Type of "f" is "Foo[int]"
  genrectst.py:8:13 - information: Type of "f.func()" is "int"
  genrectst.py:11:13 - information: Type of "g" is "Foo[Unknown]"
  genrectst.py:12:13 - information: Type of "g.func()" is "Unknown"
  genrectst.py:14:13 - error: "assert_type" mismatch: expected "Any" but received "Unknown" (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```

So with `mypy`, we can use `assert_type()` to check the result of `func()`, but how do we do this with `pyright` ?

title: Pyright ignores parameter type annotation and assigns a different type in method body.

**Describe the bug**

In the following example, pyright assigns a type different from the annotation to a parameter. This seems to happen because the parameter annotation uses a type variable that's scoped to the method's (generic) class.

**To Reproduce**

```python
from typing import Callable, Generic, TypeVar

T = TypeVar('T')
U = TypeVar('U')
V = TypeVar('V')

class F(Generic[T, U]):
    f: Callable[[T], U]

    def __init__(self, f: Callable[[T], U]):

    def __call__(self, x: T) -> U:

title: Calling with unpacked args `f(*args)` selects overload for `f()`
body_truncated:
We are seeing new Pyright failures related to the following:

```
import asyncio
from typing import Awaitable, List


async def f(a: List[Awaitable[int]]):
    b = await asyncio.gather(*a)
    reveal_type(b)  # Type of "b" is "tuple[()]"
```

The type checking now incorrectly assumes that `b` is empty, leading to potential errors down the line.

To check that this is not an issue with the `asyncio` type stubs I tried the following:

```
from typing import Any, List, Tuple, overload


@overload
def f() -> Tuple[()]:
    ...


@overload
def f(__arg1: Any) -> Tuple[bool]:
    ...


def f(*args: Any) -> Tuple[bool, ...]:
    return tuple(True for _ in args)


def g(a: List[int]):
    b = f(*a)
    reveal_type(b)  # Type of "b" is "Tuple[()]"
```

Pyright version: 1.1.258
Python version: 3.8.10

title: False positive `UnknownArgumentType` in loop
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
False positive `UnknownArgumentType` in loop.

**To Reproduce**
Don't mind the meaning of the code, it's just a minimal example I could figure out.
```py
def foo(nums: list[int], target: int) -> None:
    var = nums[0]
    while True:
        mid = var  # no error if I explicitly type `mid` here as `mid: int = var`
        if nums[mid] == target:  # Argument type is unknown/Argument corresponds to parameter "__i" in function "__getitem__"
            return
        if var:
            var = mid
        else:
            var = mid
```

**Expected behavior**
No errors.

**Screenshots or Code**
Curiously, `mid` has correct type in the tooltip.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12860284/177862997-545488e2-7701-450f-aebb-adefc701f732.png)

**VS Code extension or command-line**
I'm coming here as a Pylance user and it's present in the latest stable (2022.7.20) and preview (2022.7.21) release of Pylance. But I have checked using just the Pyright extension and it seems like it's a regression from [1.1.234](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/releases/tag/1.1.234) release of Pyright.

body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
When the `__exit__` of a context manager explicitly hints the return type of `__exit__` as `Literal[False]`, Pyright fails to assume all errors propagate outside the context manager. Without the explicit hint, it is treated correctly, and Pyright assumes all errors propagate.

Faulty report **with** explicit `Literal[False]`:
```

test.py
  test.py:17:13 - information: Type of "A.__exit__" is "(self: A, exc_type: Type[BaseException] | None, exc_value: BaseException | None, traceback: TracebackType | None) -> Literal[False]"

    Type "None" cannot be assigned to type "int" (reportGeneralTypeIssues)

pyright 1.1.257
test.py

title: Pyright does not correctly typecheck __setattr__ when calling through `=`
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

When defining a class with `__setattr__`, Pyright correctly type checks direct calls to `__setattr__`, but does not type check indirect calls to `__setattr__` through setting an attribute on an instance.

**To Reproduce**

```python
# test.py
class A:
    def __setattr__(self, key, val: int):
        pass

A().a = '1'  # this line
```

Run `pyright test.py`.
**Expected behavior**

Pyright should flag the marked `# this line` with a type error.

**Additional context**

mypy flags the line as a type error. Pytype does not.

```
test ❯ mypy test.py
test.py:5: error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "str", variable has type "int")
Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file)
```

title: `Parameter "**kwargs" has no corresponding parameter` with generic `ParamSpec`
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
When using a decorator function which is generic over the `ParamSpec` of the inner function, you will get the error: `Parameter "**kwargs" has no corresponding parameter (reportGeneralTypeIssues)`

**To Reproduce**
Here is a minimal reproduction. You can tweak a lot of the code and it will still raise this error, as long as `decorator` remains generic, using a generic `ParamSpec`.
```python
from typing import Callable, Any, ParamSpec

Params = ParamSpec("Params")
Call = Callable[Params, Any]

def decorator(func: Call) -> Call:
    return func

@decorator
def foo():
    pass
```

**Expected behavior**
I don't think this should not throw an error. The only thing I'm unsure about is whether it's valid to use `Call` as though it's a generic `TypeVar` when it isn't exactly that. If my usage is invalid, then it would be better for this warning to explain that, rather than throw this misleading error about `**kwargs`.

title: `_` redefinition check raises new errors
body_truncated:
In Pyright 1.1.256, we've found that many new errors are being reported for `_` in our code base, probably because of the change in 9bad0897c642d0e2bdf859cd10c09038c6416e2f.

```
 error: Function declaration "_" is obscured by a declaration of the same name (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```

This is because we are using `_` as a placeholder name for registering callbacks. The code in question is something like this:

```py
from typing import Callable

callback_registry: list[Callable[[], None]] = []

def register(fn: Callable[[], None]) -> None:
    callback_registry.append(fn)

@register
def _():
    print("Callback 1 called")

@register
def _():
    print("Callback 2 called")
```

When run through pyright 1.1.256, it says:

```
..../test.py:11:5 - error: Function declaration "_" is obscured by a declaration of the same name (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
1 error, 0 warnings, 0 informations 
```

In our use case, we're not actually using the name `_` -- we just had to give the function _some_ name because Python doesn't support anonymous functions with more than one line.

Is it intentional that pyright will report an error in cases like this?

title: Pyright 1.1.256 Not Associating total_ordering decorated class as member of isinstance check.
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Beginning with the latest release of Pyright (1.1.256), it looks like the isinstance check is no longer correctly identifying the type of the object when used with functools.total_ordering.
Back-leveling to Pyright 1.1.255 will resolve the issue, as will removing the total_ordering decorator from the class.

**To Reproduce**
Run the code below on Pyright 1.1.256 command line.
It results in the following errors:
1.   Cannot access member "value" for type "object"  Member "value" is unknown (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
2.   Type of "value" is unknown (reportUnknownMemberType)
3.   Return type is unknown (reportUnknownVariableType)
4.   Cannot access member "value" for type "object"

**Expected behavior**
The isinstance check should correctly associate the object as a member of the checked type.

**Screenshots or Code**
```python
import functools

@functools.total_ordering
class Foo:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.value: int = 0

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Foo):
            return NotImplemented

        return self.value == other.value

    def __le__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Foo):
            return NotImplemented

        return self.value <= other.value
```


**VS Code extension or command-line**
Command-line at version 1.1.256

title: Inconsistency when typechecking dunders
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
CPython will look up dunder methods among any attributes that are implemented by descriptors. In the standard case a dunder method would be implemented by a `def` within the class body, so the function object is acting as a descriptor. However it is also possible to use e.g. `__slots__`, in which case a `member_descriptor` is used.

From the above it follows that the following thing will fail:
```python
class C:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__iter__ = lambda: iter([])
        self.__add__ = lambda x: x

for _ in C(): pass # TypeError: 'C' object is not iterable
C() + C() # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'C' and 'C'
```
However the following thing will succeed:
```python
class D:
    __slots__ = "__iter__", "__add__"
    def __init__(self):
        self.__iter__ = lambda: iter([])
        self.__add__ = lambda x: x

for _ in D(): pass
D() + D()
```

**To Reproduce**
Running pyright on both snippets reveals that pyright thinks that both types are addable but neither is iterable:
```

title: `Literal` type is widened in a lambda expression when originating from iteration over `dict.items()`
body_truncated:
Pyright widens `Literal` type when used in a lambda expression when the source of the `Literal` type is the key and value from a `dict.items()` expression.

Example code:

```py
from typing import Literal

def some_func(some_dict: dict[Literal["hello"], Literal[5]]):
    for hello, five in some_dict.items():
        reveal_type(hello)  # Type of "hello" is "Literal['hello']"

        reveal_type(five)  # Type of "five" is "Literal[5]"
        lambda x: reveal_type(five)  # Type of "five" is "int"
```

~The `Literal` type does not get widened when iterating over either `dict.keys()` or `dict.values()` or when iterating over other iterable types as far as I've noticed, although I have not conducted an exhaustive search.~

Mypy in this case retains the `Literal` type, and I would expect pyright to do the same.

title: Handling of unbound TypeVars from external libraries
body_truncated:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
I'm using the library [RxPy](https://github.com/ReactiveX/RxPY)(v. 4.0.0) for some stream processing and have ran into an interesting case of unbounded `TypeVar`s, similar to [this issue](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/issues/2253).

This is the signature of the function I'm calling:
```python
_T = TypeVar("_T")
_TKey = TypeVar("_TKey")
_TValue = TypeVar("_TValue")

def group_by(
    key_mapper: Mapper[_T, _TKey],
    element_mapper: Optional[Mapper[_T, _TValue]] = None,
    subject_mapper: Optional[Callable[[], Subject[_TValue]]] = None,
) -> Callable[[Observable[_T]], Observable[GroupedObservable[_TKey, _TValue]]]:
...
```
As you can see, the `element_mapper` and `subject_mapper` parameters are optional, making `_TValue` unbound. 

Using a result of the call to this function would make pyright report an error like this:

```
Type "_TValue@group_by" cannot be assigned to type "Dict[Unknown, Unknown]"
```
The type of the error falls under the `reportGeneralTypeIssues` category.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Comparing my problem to the above-linked issue, the main difference is that I can't modify the used code easily.
Libraries aside, wouldn't it make sense to assume every unbound generics parameter as `Unknown` or `Any`? 
In cases like these, no type can be inferred, and the consumer of the function cannot do anything with the info the error provides.
If the signature of the function is invalid, a separate error should reside there in my opinion.

If this is not feasible, it would be nice to have a separate category for unbound `TypeVars` and allow the user to suppress them or handle the case explicitly.

title: Protocol is incorrectly shown as compatible
Generic protocol is incorrectly shown as incompatible under certain cases
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
A class which should be marked as implementing a generic protocol is not identified as such.

**To Reproduce**
```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar, Union, Protocol

T = TypeVar("T")
U = TypeVar("U")

class X(Generic[T, U], Protocol):
    def f(self) -> Union[T, U]:
        ...

    def g(self) -> "X[T, U]":
        ...

class Y(Generic[T, U]):
    def f(self) -> Union[T, U]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def g(self) -> X[T, U]:
        return Y[T, U]()
```

results in the following: 
```
error: Expression of type "Y[U@Y, T@Y]" cannot be assigned to return type "X[T@Y, U@Y]"
    "Y[U@Y, T@Y]" is incompatible with protocol "X[T@Y, U@Y]"
      TypeVar "T@X" is invariant
        Type "U@Y" cannot be assigned to type "T@Y" (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```

The following variation results in a different error:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Generic, TypeVar, Union, Protocol

T = TypeVar("T")
U = TypeVar("U")

class X(Generic[T, U], Protocol):
    def f(self) -> Union[T, U]:
        ...

    def g(self, tu: Union[T, U]) -> "X[T, U]":
        ...

@dataclass
class Y(Generic[T, U]):
    tu: Union[T, U]
    def f(self) -> Union[T, U]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def g(self, tu: Union[T, U]) -> X[T, U]:
        return Y[T, U](tu)
```

The error is
```
error: Expression of type "Y[T@Y, U@Y]" cannot be assigned to return type "X[T@Y, U@Y]"
    "Y[T@Y, U@Y]" is incompatible with protocol "X[T@Y, U@Y]"
      "g" is an incompatible type
        Type "(tu: T@Y | U@Y) -> X[T@Y, U@Y]" cannot be assigned to type "(tu: T@X | U@X) -> X[T@X, U@X]"
          Function return type "X[T@Y, U@Y]" is incompatible with type "X[T@X, U@X]"
            TypeVar "T@X" is invariant (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```

Replacing `Union` with `Dict`, removing `f`, or changing the return type of `f` to something else like `T` or `U` all cause the error to go away.

title: Decorator changes signature of function that uses `TypeVar`
body_truncated: This is a bit hard to describe, so I'll illustrate with an example. `f` is a function which takes two parameters, of types `T` and `Union[T, List[T]]`. When we use `f()` and pass in those different types, the type checker correctly says that it's OK (no red underlining): ```py from typing import Callable, TypeVar, Union, List, Any T = TypeVar("T", int, str) def f(x: T, y: Union[T, List[T]]) -> None: pass f(1, 2) # OK f(1, [2, 3]) # OK ``` Now, let's say we have a decorator which returns a function of type `Callable[[U], U]`. (Imagine, for example, that this decorator is used to modify a docstring.) If that decorator is used on a function identical to `f`, then Pylance thinks that the signature of the resulting function has changed, and flags spurious errors. ```py U = TypeVar("U") def doc() -> Callable[[U], U]: ... @doc() def g(x: T, y: Union[T, List[T]]) -> None: pass g(1, 2) # `2` is underlined g(1, [2, 3]) # OK ``` Here's a screenshot: When I hover over the `2`, I see this text: ``` Argument of type "Literal[2]" cannot be assigned to parameter "y" of type "List[T@g]" in function "g" "Literal[2]" is incompatible with "List[T@g]" ``` This is with Pylance v2022.4.1 . ***** Some notes: The specific `doc` decorator above could be rewritten so that it could be used as `@doc` instead of `@doc()`, and that does make the error go away. title: Generic variadic callable annotation is not enforced (PEP 646).
body_truncated:
Pyright (CLI 1.1.236)
```py
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar, Callable, Protocol, Any
from typing_extensions import Unpack

class SupportsSum(Protocol):
    def __add__(self, __x: Any) -> Any: ...
    
T = TypeVar('T', bound=SupportsSum)

def wrapped_summation(start: T) -> Callable[[Unpack[tuple[T, ...]]], T]:
    def inner_func(*values: T):
        return sum(values, start=start)

    return inner_func

float_sum = wrapped_summation(0.0)
int_sum = wrapped_summation(3)

reveal_type(float_sum)  # Type of "float_sum" is "(*tuple[float, ...]) -> float"
reveal_type(int_sum)    # Type of "int_sum" is "(*tuple[int, ...]) -> int"

int_sum(None)  # ERROR Type "None" cannot be assigned to type "SupportsSum"
int_sum(3.14, 42.0)  # No errors
```
Pyright seems to only enforce the TypeVar bound, but not the type inferred. `int_sum(3.14, 42.0)` should be an error, unless this type of construction isn't going to be supported since you can achieve the same with a Protocol

class VariadicCallable(Protocol[T_contra, T_co]):
    def __call__(self, *args: T_contra) -> T_co: ...

title: Nested decorators with ParamSpec no longer support args and kwargs attributes
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**

In the newest release, nested decorators no longer support `P.args` and `P.kwargs`.

**To Reproduce**
Have a decorator that returns a callable that wraps another callable and have it use `ParamSpec` attributes.

Running pyright on this results in an error:

2 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations

No error.

from typing_extensions import ParamSpec

T = TypeVar('T')

title: Concatenate Paramspec False Negatives
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
The code below has a buggy decorator that does not pass *args/**kwargs appropriately. It does not give any type errors though. 

```python
from typing import Callable

from typing_extensions import Concatenate, ParamSpec

P = ParamSpec("P")


def dec(func: Callable[Concatenate[int, P], int]) -> Callable[Concatenate[int, P], int]:
    # No Error reported here.
    def _func(x: int) -> int:
        return func(x)  # Expect 1 error here for bad call

    return _func # Expect 2nd error here as _func does not contain P in its signature


def add_k(x: int, k: int) -> int:
    return x + k


dec(add_k)(1, 3) # Crashes
```

The issue partly requires Concatenate. The first missing error does appear if you remove concatenate,

```python

def dec(func: Callable[P, int]) -> Callable[P, int]:
    def _func(x: int) -> int:
        return func(x) # Good error reported

    return _func # Weird, no error here
```

but you can simplify more and have no errors reported even though it'll still crash if you try to use it,

```python

def dec(func: Callable[P, int]) -> Callable[P, int]:
    def _func(x: int) -> int:
        return 3

    return _func # No error
```

So I think there's 2 related issues here.

**Expected behavior**
Errors to be reported when decorator doesn't forward arguments.

**VS Code extension or command-line**
pyright 1.1.235

title: Paramspec issue in generic class with __init__
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
I have a small collection of examples of unexpected type errors/lack of type errors when using generic class with paramspec and P.args/P.kwargs on `__init__`.

```python
from typing import Callable, Generic, TypeVar

from typing_extensions import Concatenate, ParamSpec

P = ParamSpec("P")
T1 = TypeVar("T1")
T2 = TypeVar("T2")


def add_k(x: int, k: int) -> int:
    return x + k


class BadExecute1(Generic[P, T2]):
    def __init__(self, fn: Callable[P, T2], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> None:
        self.fn = fn
        self.args = args
        self.kwargs = kwargs

    def __call__(self) -> T2:
        return self.fn(*self.args, **self.kwargs)


bad_processor1 = BadExecute1(add_k)  # No type errors when there should be 1 for missing x/k.
print(bad_processor1())

bad_processor2 = BadExecute1(add_k, x=3, k=2)  # Two false positive type errors of no parameter x/k.
print(bad_processor2())


class BadExecute2(Generic[P, T1, T2]):
    def __init__(self, fn: Callable[Concatenate[T1, P], T2], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> None:
        self.fn = fn
        self.args = args
        self.kwargs = kwargs

    def __call__(self, value: T1) -> T2:
        return self.fn(value, *self.args, **self.kwargs)


bad_processor3 = BadExecute2(add_k)  # No type error even though k is missing.
print(bad_processor3(1))

bad_processor4 = BadExecute2(add_k, k=2)  # False positive error of no parameter named k.
print(bad_processor4(1))

title: Treatment of Hashable in invariant type argument
body_truncated:
Consider this example (checked in latest Pylance in VSCode, as always):

```python
from typing import Hashable


def f(x: list[Hashable]):
    x.append("x")


def g(x: list[object]):
    pass


l: list[int] = [1]
f(l)  # no error
g(l)  # error (as expected)
```

`f(l)` should be an error, because `list[]` is invariant and `f` wants a `list[Hashable]`, not `list[int]`. It errors correctly when the callee is annotated as `list[object]` instead.

Context: https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/12464#issuecomment-1079759274

title: Dataclass field that contains a descriptor object isn't handled correctly
body_truncated:
If a `@dataclass` field is initialized with a descriptor as a default value, pyright should use the value type of the `__set__` method for the descriptor when determining the type of the corresponding parameter within the synthesized `__init__` method. 

Types are also evaluated incorrectly in this case.

Note that mypy also exhibits these same bugs.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, cast


class MyDescriptor:
    def __get__(self, __obj: object | None, __owner: Any) -> "int | MyDescriptor":
        if __obj is None:
            return self
        return cast(Any, __obj)._x

body_truncated:
`pyright --verifytypes` appears to think that unannotated functions with a single parameter have known type:

```
# foo/__init__.py in a py.typed package `foo`
def foo(bar) -> str:

Symbols exported by "fakepkg": 1

  With ambiguous type: 0
  With unknown type: 0

title: Variance and Nested Protocols
body_truncated:
When using a certain set of nested protocols, pyright declares a seemingly correct implementation of that protocol incorrect due to variance issues. In particular:
```py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol, TypeVar

X = TypeVar("X", covariant=True)
Y = TypeVar("Y", contravariant=True)
Z = TypeVar("Z")

class Fn(Protocol[Y]):
    def __call__(self, y: Y) -> None: ...
class FnHandler(Protocol[X]):
    def __call__(self, x: Fn[X]) -> None: ...
def handler(x: Fn[int]) -> None: ...

class ModuleSpec(Protocol[Z]):
    x: FnHandler[Z]
@dataclass
class Module:
    x = handler

h: FnHandler[int] = Module().x
m: ModuleSpec[int] = Module() # error here
```
produces an error on the final line:
```
 error: Expression of type "Module" cannot be assigned to declared type "ModuleSpec[int]"
    "Module" is incompatible with protocol "ModuleSpec[int]"
      "x" is an incompatible type
        Type "(x: Fn[int]) -> None" cannot be assigned to type "(x: Fn[Z@ModuleSpec]) -> None"
          Parameter 1: type "Fn[Z@ModuleSpec]" cannot be assigned to type "Fn[int]"
            TypeVar "Y@Fn" is contravariant (reportGeneralTypeIssues)
```
This seems pretty surprising given that the line immediately above it type checks fine and all `Module` is doing is passing an invariant `TypeVar` down to the single member. A further curiosity is that the following code does type check wherein we ignore the demand to make our `TypeVar` contravariant:

```py

from typing import Protocol, TypeVar

Z = TypeVar("Z")

class FnHandler2(Protocol[Z]):
    def __call__(self, x: Fn2[Z]) -> None: ...
def handler2(x: Fn[int]) -> None: ...

class ModuleSpec2(Protocol[Z]):
    x: FnHandler2[Z]
@dataclass
class Module2:

title: Resolution of type[T] using TypeVar with parent & child class as constraints is order-dependent
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
When a `TypeVar` constrained by two related types, e.g. `class A` and `class B(A)`, is used inside `type[T]`, the type that `T` resolves to depends on the order in which the constraints are provided. Specifically, if `T` could resolve to more than one of the constrained types, the leftmost one is chosen.

As far as I can tell, this only occurs with `type[T]`, and plain `T` resolves as expected.

**To Reproduce**
Given a function `type[T] -> type[T]` with a `TypeVar("T", A, B)` as described, provide a value of type `type[B]` as its parameter. The return type is inferred as `type[A]`. If the order of the constraints is reversed, it is inferred as `type[B]`.

**Expected behavior**
The most specific type satisfying the arguments and constraints should be picked regardless of order, in this case `type[B]`.

**Screenshots or Code**
Here is a demonstration of the problem:
```python
class A:...
class B(A):...

T = TypeVar("T", A, B)
U = TypeVar("U", B, A)

def foo(t: type[T]) -> type[T]: return t
def bar(u: type[U]) -> type[U]: return u

FooB = foo(B)
BarB = bar(B)

reveal_type(FooB) # Type of "FooB" is "Type[A]"
reveal_type(BarB) # Type of "BarB" is "Type[B]"
```

**VS Code extension or command-line**
I have tried both the extension (`Pylance  v2022.3.0`) and the command-line (`pyright 1.1.227`).

**Additional context**
This issue can be mitigated in code by arranging the most specific constraints first.

title: Incorrect assessment of exhausting matching for tuple with literal values
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
Variations on tuple matching arms can be constructed to report both false positive inexhaustive and false negative exhaustive matches:

```python
# pyright reports:
# Cases within match statement do not exhaustively handle all values
#  Unhandled type: "tuple[Literal[0]]"
match (0,):
    # however, this arm matches
    case (0,):
        print(1)

# equivalent to the above, to the best of my understanding, but no error
match (0,):
    case tuple((0,)):
        print(2)

# however, we can also construct a false negative
match (0,):
    # this arm does not match, but no error is reported
    case tuple((1,)):
        print(3)

match (0,):
    # pyright catches the problem in this construction:
    # Condition will always evaluate to False since the types "Literal[0]" and
    # "Literal[1]" have no overlap
    case tuple((foo,)) if foo == 1:
        print(4)

# but incorrectly reports inexhaustive matching here
match (0,):
    case tuple((foo,)) if foo == 0:
        print(5)


def match_tuple(tup: tuple[int]):
    # the tuple((literal,)) construction is also allowed when we have no
    # information about the value being matched
    match tup:
        case tuple((1,)):
            print(6)


match_tuple((0,))
match_tuple((1,))

# out:
# 1
# 2
# 5
# 6
```

**To Reproduce**
Paste the above into VS Code and observe which constructions are accepted and rejected.

**Expected behavior**
Cases 1, 2, and 5 should be accepted, and 3, 4, and 6 should be rejected (and for the right reason).

**VS Code extension or command-line**

pyright: 1.1.226

I have descriptor that I set to the result of a method call (more specifically `contextlib.ExitStack.enter_context()`) but Pyright complains that the result of the method has incompatible types with the attribute/descriptor.

title: Add better heuristic for imports within `try` statement
body_truncated:
Several pylance users have reported unexpected "unreachable code" when using one of several untyped libraries. These libraries are attempting to import yet another library. The import statement is located within a `try` block, and the `except` logic builds a minimal replacement for the imported library that always raises exceptions.

Pyright's current heuristics for resolving imports chooses the last declaration in a source file. We should explore using the last declaration that is not within an `except` handler.

See https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release/issues/2402 for the original bug report and code samples.

title: Wildcard import from stub should not include symbols beginning with underscore
body_truncated: With stub files, symbols that begin with an underscore are designed to be "externally visible" (i.e. not considered "private"). However, if you use a wildcard import from the stub, these symbols are still supposed to be treated as private and not included in the import.

title: Structural pattern match of self over self's class incorrectly reports inexhaustive match
body_truncated:
**Describe the bug**
When using structural pattern matching on `self` in an instance method, pyright reports, 'Cases within match statement do not exhaustively handle all values. Unhandled type: "Self@CLASS_NAME"...'

**To Reproduce**
The most basic case is something like the following:
```python
class Foo:
    def __str__(self) -> str:
        match self:
            case Foo(): return "baz"
```
However, there is little practical reason to do such a thing, so here is the motivating application using `Enum`s:
```python
from enum import Enum, auto


class Foo(Enum):
    bar = auto()

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        match self:
            case Foo.bar:
                return "bar"
```

In either case, pyright reports, 'Unhandled type: "Self@Foo".' Running e.g. `print(f"{Foo.bar}")` prints "bar" as expected.

Two notes:
1. Adding `assert isinstance(self, Foo)` above the `match` statement quiets the error. Annotating `self: Foo` does the same.
2. Seemingly related is the alternate formulation `if self is Foo.bar: return "bar"`, for which pyright complains, "Function with declared type of "str" must return value." Curiously, adding an assertion to that formulation does *not* quiet the error, although annotating `self` does.

**Expected behavior**
The type checker should recognize that `self`, being an instance of `Foo`, can only be `Foo.bar`. It's unclear to me what `Self@CLASS_NAME` as the type denotes (why isn't the type just the class?), but some incongruity between the `Self@` type and the class type seems to be at the heart of the issue.

**VS Code extension or command-line**
Pylance v2022.2.1

"verifytypes" flags unannotated class or instance variable as untyped when parent class provides annotation
body_truncated:
When a "py.typed" library annotates a class or instance variable in a base class, it shouldn't need to re-declare the type in subclasses. Pyright already properly handles this case during type evaluation, but its "verifytypes" feature still flags the resulting class and instance variables in the subclasses as "unknown types". This forces library authors to add needless annotations in the child classes if they want to silence the errors emitted by "verifytypes".

This bug should be fixed in the "verifytypes" tool and the guidance document should be updated to document this case.

I'm working with a 3rd party library that uses a sentinel object to detect default value usage on an Optional initializer parameter. However, when I attempt to concatenate two lists of these objects with the `+` operator, I'm getting a error reported by Pyright and Pylance.

Reproducible code:

```python

from typing import List

_DEFAULT_VALUE = object()

class MyClass(object):

    def __init__(
        self,
        name,
        description=_DEFAULT_VALUE,
    ):
        ...

X: List[MyClass] = [MyClass("a", description="b")]
Y: List[MyClass] = [MyClass("c")]
Z: List[MyClass] = X + Y # Operator "+" not supported for types "list[MyClass]" and "list[MyClass]"
```

The error is shown on the last line `Operator "+" not supported for types "list[MyClass]" and "list[MyClass]"`

The interesting part is if I remove the `description` param when assigning the list to `X` in the example above, the error goes away. 

Pyright 1.1.220 and Pylance v2022.2.0 on MacOS

title: Performance Regression 2 Recursive Types
Constrained `TypeVar`s can be resolved to subclasses of constraints
body_truncated:
According to PEP 484, if a type variable is constrained, it can only be assigned to the explicitly listed types, not to any of the subtypes.

However, it seems like this restriction doesn't work when explicitly specifying the type in brackets.

```py
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

class A: ...
class B: ...
class A2(A): ...
T = TypeVar("T", A, B)

class F(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, thing: T) -> None:
        self.thing = thing

f1 = F(A2())
reveal_type(f1)  # F[A], which is correct
reveal_type(f1.thing)  # A, which is correct

f2 = F[A2](A2())
reveal_type(f2)  # F[A2], incorrect
reveal_type(f2.thing)  # A2, incorrect
```
Another example would be with a contravariant type variable:
```py
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

class A: ...
class B: ...
class A2(A): ...

T = TypeVar("T", A, B, contravariant=True)

class F(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, thing: Callable[[T], None]) -> None:
        self.thing = thing

def callback(a: A) -> None:
    ...

f1: F[A2] = F(callback)
reveal_type(f1)  # F[A2]
reveal_type(f1.thing)  # (A2) -> None
```
Here, the type of `F(callback)` is inferred as `F[A]` correctly, but the explicit annotation makes `f1` have the type `F[A2]`. 

Shouldn't `F[A2]` be prohibited in general? Or am I misunderstanding PEP 484?

title: `Iterable` incorrectly evaluated as always truthy
body_truncated:
Pyright version: v1.1.219

```py
from collections.abc import Iterable

def f(foo: Iterable[int]) -> None:
    if foo:
        print(sum(foo))
        reveal_type(foo)  # Iterable[int]
    else:
        reveal_type(foo)  # Never
```
This doesn't seem right: there are definitely iterables which are falsey.
(admittedly, checking `Iterable` for truthiness doesn't make much sense to me. maybe there's a better example?)

However, if you explicitly define `__bool__` on the type, it does work correctly
```py
import random
from typing import TypeVar, Generic
from collections.abc import Iterable


T = TypeVar("T")


class CoolIterable(Iterable[T], Generic[T]):
    def __bool__(self) -> bool:
        return random.random() > 0.5


def f(foo: CoolIterable[int]) -> None:
    if foo:
        print(sum(foo))
        reveal_type(foo)
    else:
        reveal_type(foo)
```

---

Possibly related to #3005 ?

body_truncated:

title: Regression in 1.1.194 involving mapping-values w/ recursive types
body_truncated:
`Mapping[Any, <Recursive-Type>]` is not checked accurately; it permits false negatives, as demonstrated below. It appears that this is a regression that was introduced in pyright 1.1.194, and it persists up through 1.1.218.

```python
from typing import Union, Mapping, Any

A = Union[str, int]
B = Union[A, Mapping[Any, "B"]]


class M:
    pass


def g(x: B):
    return


# (pyright 1.1.193) error: Argument of type "dict[Any, M]" cannot be assigned to parameter "x" of type "B"
# (pyright 1.1.[194-218]) no error
g({1: M()})
```
